vsm1.1:16.1:
However, even when this path of purification is shown in this way under the headings of virtue,
concentration and understanding, each comprising various special qualities,
vsm1.1:16.2: it is still only shown extremely briefly.
vsm1.1:16.3: And so since that is insufficient to help all,
vsm1.1:16.4: there is, in order to show it in detail, the following set of questions dealing in the first place with virtue:
vsm1.1:16.5: (i) What is virtue? (ii) In what sense is it virtue?
vsm1.1:16.6: (iii) What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? (iv) What are the benefits of virtue?
vsm1.1:16.7: (v) How many kinds of virtue are there? (vi) What is the defiling of it? (viii) What is the cleansing of it?
vsm1.1:17.3:
It is the states beginning with volition present in one who abstains from killing living things,
etc., or in one who fulfils the practice of the duties.
vsm1.1:17.4: For this is said in the Paṭisambhidā: “What is virtue? There is virtue as volition, virtue as consciousness-concomitant,
vsm1.1:17.5: virtue as restraint, virtue as non-transgression” (Paṭis I 44).
vsm1.1:17.6:
Herein, virtue as volition is the volition present in one who abstains from killing living things,
etc., or in one who fulfils the practice of the duties.
vsm1.1:17.7: Virtue as consciousness-concomitant is the abstinence in one who abstains from killing living things, and so on.
vsm1.1:17.8:
Furthermore, virtue as volition is the seven volitions that accompany the first seven of the ten
courses of action (kamma) in one who abandons the killing of living things, and so on.
vsm1.1:17.9:
Virtue as consciousness-concomitant is the three remaining states consisting of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view,
stated in the way beginning, “Abandoning covetousness, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness” (D I 71).
vsm1.1:18.1:
Virtue as restraint should be understood here as restraint in five ways:
restraint by the rules of the community (pātimokkha), restraint by mindfulness,
vsm1.1:18.2: restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy.
vsm1.1:18.3: Herein, “restraint by the Pātimokkha” is this: “He is furnished, fully furnished, with this Pātimokkha restraint” (Vibh 246).
vsm1.1:18.4: “Restraint by mindfulness” is this: “He guards the eye faculty, enters upon restraint of the eye faculty” (D I 70).
vsm1.1:18.5:
“Restraint by knowledge” is this: “The currents in the world that flow, Ajita,” said the Blessed
One, “are stemmed by means of mindfulness; restraint of currents I proclaim, by understanding they are dammed” (Sn 1035);
vsm1.1:18.7: And use of requisites is here combined with this.
vsm1.1:18.8: But what is called “restraint by patience” is that given in the way beginning, “He is one who bears cold and heat” (M I 10).
vsm1.1:18.9:
And what is called “restraint by energy” is that given in the way beginning,
“He does not endure a thought of sense desires when it arises” (M I 11);
vsm1.1:18.10: purification of livelihood is here combined with this.
vsm1.1:18.11: So this fivefold restraint, and the abstinence, in clansmen who dread evil, from any chance of transgression met with,
vsm1.1:18.12: should all be understood to be “virtue as restraint.”
vsm1.1:18.13: Virtue as non-transgression is the non-transgression, by body or speech, of precepts of virtue that have been undertaken.
vsm1.1:18.14: This, in the first place, is the answer to the question, “What is virtue?”
vsm1.1:19.1: Now, as to the rest— (ii) IN WHAT SENSE IS IT VIRTUE? It is virtue (sīla) in the sense of composing (sīlana).
vsm1.1:19.3: It is either a coordinating (samādhāna), meaning non-inconsistency of bodily action, etc., due to virtuousness;
vsm1.1:19.4: or it is an upholding (upadhāraṇa), meaning a state of basis (ādhāra) owing to its serving as foundation for profitable states.
vsm1.1:19.5: For those who understand etymology admit only these two meanings.
vsm1.1:19.6:
Others, however, comment on the meaning here in the way beginning, “The meaning of virtue (sīla)
is the meaning of head (sira), the meaning of virtue is the meaning of cool (sītala).”
vsm1.1:20.1: (iii) Now, WHAT ARE ITS CHARACTERISTIC, FUNCTION, MANIFESTATION, AND PROXIMATE CAUSE? Here:
vsm1.1:20.2:
The characteristic of it is composing, even when analyzed in various ways,
as visibility is of visible data even when analyzed in various ways.
vsm1.1:20.3:
Just as visibleness is the characteristic of the visible-data base even when
analyzed into the various categories of blue, yellow, etc.,
vsm1.1:20.4: because even when analyzed into these categories it does not exceed visible-ness,
vsm1.1:20.5:
so also this same composing, described above as the coordinating of bodily action, etc., and as the foundation of profitable
states, is the characteristic of virtue even when analyzed into the various categories of volition, etc.,
vsm1.1:20.6: because even when analyzed into these categories it does not exceed the state of coordination and foundation.
vsm1.1:21.2: Its function has a double sense, as action, to stop misconduct, and as achievement, the quality of blamelessness in virtuous men.
vsm1.1:21.3:
So what is called virtue should be understood to have the function (nature) of stopping
misconduct as its function (nature) in the sense of action,
vsm1.1:21.4: and a blameless function (nature) as its function (nature) in the sense of achievement.
vsm1.1:21.5:
For under these headings of characteristic, etc., it is action (kicca) or it is achievement
(sampatti) that is called “function” (rasa—nature).
vsm1.1:22.1:
Now, virtue, so say those who know, shows itself as purity; and for its proximate
cause they tell the pair, conscience and shame, as well.
vsm1.1:22.2: This virtue is manifested as the kinds of purity stated thus: “Bodily purity, verbal purity, mental purity” (A I 271);
vsm1.1:22.3: it is manifested, comes to be apprehended, as a pure state.
vsm1.1:22.4: But conscience and shame are said by those who know to be its proximate cause; its near reason, is the meaning.
vsm1.1:22.5: For when conscience and shame are in existence, virtue arises and persists;
vsm1.1:22.6: and when they are not, it neither arises nor persists.
vsm1.1:22.7: This is how virtue's characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause, should be understood.
vsm1.1:23.2: 23. (iv) WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS OF VIRTUE?
vsm1.1:23.3: Its benefits are the acquisition of the several special qualities beginning with non-remorse.
vsm1.1:23.4: For this is said: “Ānanda, profitable habits (virtues) have non-remorse as their aim and non-remorse as their benefit” (A V 1).
vsm1.1:23.5: Also it is said further: “Householder, there are these five benefits for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.
vsm1.1:23.7: Here, householder, one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, obtains a large fortune as a consequence of diligence;
vsm1.1:23.8: this is the first benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.
vsm1.1:23.9: Again, of one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, a fair name is spread abroad;
vsm1.1:23.10: this is the second benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.
vsm1.1:23.11:
Again, whenever one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, enters an assembly,
whether of khattiyas (warrior-nobles) or brahmans or householders or ascetics,
vsm1.1:23.12: he does so without fear or hesitation;
vsm1.1:23.13: this is the third benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.
vsm1.1:23.14: Again, one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, dies unconfused;
vsm1.1:23.15: this is the fourth benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue.
vsm1.1:23.16:
Again, one who is virtuous, possessed of virtue, on the breakup of the body, after death,
reappears in a happy destiny, in the heavenly world;
vsm1.1:23.17: this is the fifth benefit for the virtuous in the perfecting of virtue” (D II 86).
vsm1.1:23.18:
There are also the many benefits of virtue beginning with being dear and loved and ending with destruction of cankers
described in the passage beginning, “If a bhikkhu should wish, ‘May I be dear to my fellows in the life of purity and loved by them,
held in respect and honoured by them,’ let him perfect the virtues” (M I 33).
vsm1.1:23.19: This is how virtue has as its benefits the several special qualities beginning with non-remorse.
vsm1.1:24.2: Dare anyone a limit place On benefits that virtue brings, Without which virtue clansmen find No footing in the dispensation?
vsm1.1:24.3: No Ganges, and no Yamunā No Sarabhū, Sarassathī, Or flowing Aciravatī, Or noble River of Mahī,
vsm1.1:24.4:
Is able to wash out the stain In things that breathe here in the world; For only
virtue's water can Wash out the stain in living things.
vsm1.1:24.5: No breezes that come bringing rain, No balm of yellow sandalwood, No necklaces beside, or gems Or soft effulgence of moonbeams,
vsm1.1:24.6:
Can here avail to calm and soothe Men's fevers in this world; whereas This noble,
this supremely cool, Well-guarded virtue quells the flame.
vsm1.1:24.7: Where is there to be found the scent That can with virtue's scent compare, And that is borne against the wind As easily as with it?
vsm1.1:24.8:
Where Can such another stair be found That climbs, as virtue does, to heaven? Or yet
another door that gives Onto the City of Nibbāna?
vsm1.1:24.9:
Shine as they may, there are no kings Adorned with jewellery and pearls That shine
as does a man restrained Adorned with virtue's ornament.
vsm1.1:24.10: Virtue entirely does away With dread of self-blame and the like; Their virtue to the virtuous Gives gladness always by its fame.
vsm1.1:24.11:
From this brief sketch it may be known How virtue brings reward, and how This
root of all good qualities Robs of its power every fault.
